w: The largest naval base in Western Europe began in the 1690s when Edmund Dummer built one of the world's earliest stepped stone dry docks here on open ground. More than 300 naval vessels were built at the yard before shipbuilding stopped in the late 1960s; today it is the Royal Navy's only nuclear repair and refuelling facility.
s: Western Europe's biggest naval base, building ships since the 1690s
_facts: Founded in the late 17th century by Edmund Dummer with an early stepped stone dry dock
Over 300 naval vessels built here; last was HMS Scylla in 1968
Sole nuclear repair and refuelling facility for the Royal Navy
Known as HM Dockyard, Plymouth until renamed Devonport in 1843

w: A Churchill-class nuclear submarine that served the Royal Navy from 1971, Courageous is now preserved as a museum ship at the Devonport Naval Heritage Centre. Plans launched in 2021, backed by the National Museum of the Royal Navy, aim to build a Cold War Centre around her.
s: A Cold War nuclear submarine turned museum piece
_facts: Churchill-class nuclear fleet submarine, in service from 1971
Now a museum ship at the Devonport Naval Heritage Centre
Cold War Centre plans began in 2021 with the National Museum of the Royal Navy

w: Plymouth's original harbour district survived both the Blitz and the slum clearances that erased so much of the city's old fabric. Its streets hold the largest concentration of cobbled streets in Britain and around 100 listed buildings, with Southside Street and The Barbican itself still lined mostly with pubs and restaurants.
s: The old harbour quarter that dodged the Blitz
_facts: Original harbour of Plymouth, around Sutton Harbour
Escaped most Blitz destruction and Victorian slum clearance
Largest concentration of cobbled streets in Britain
About 100 listed buildings

w: The Edgcumbe family laid out temples, follies and formal gardens here from the 18th century onward, overlooking Plymouth Sound from the Cornish shore. The South West Coast Path runs nine miles through the park, past a herd of wild fallow deer and specimen giant sequoias, with the Italian, French, English and Jubilee Gardens free to enter year-round.
s: Follies, giant sequoias and wild deer across the Sound
_facts: Grade I listed, 885-acre country park on the Rame Peninsula
South West Coast Path runs 9 miles through the park
Formal Gardens include Italian, French, English and Jubilee gardens
Free admission year-round

w: On Plymouth Hoe, this war memorial commemorates British and Commonwealth sailors of both World Wars who have no known grave, their names recorded here in place of a headstone the sea never gave them.
s: Names of sailors the sea never returned
_facts: War memorial on Plymouth Hoe
Commemorates British and Commonwealth sailors of WWI and WWII with no known grave

w: Licensed for services in 1371, this garrison church inside the Royal Citadel was demolished and rebuilt between 1666 and 1671, then given galleries and transepts in 1845 that turned its plan into a symmetrical cross. George V re-granted it Royal Chapel status in 1927, and it still serves as garrison church to the Royal Artillery and 29 Commando.
s: A 14th-century chapel garrisoned inside the Citadel
_facts: Licensed for services in 1371 by the Bishop of Exeter
Rebuilt 1666-1671; galleries and transepts added in 1845
Re-granted Royal Chapel title by George V in 1927
Garrison church to the Royal Artillery and 29 Commando

w: Opened in 1858 under the patronage of the Virgin Mary and St Boniface, a local saint thought born nearby in Crediton, this Roman Catholic cathedral serves a diocese spanning Cornwall, Devon and Dorset. Royal Navy personnel from HMNB Devonport still gather here every July for the annual naval mass.
s: A cathedral that hosts the navy's annual mass
_facts: Opened 1858, seat of the Bishop of Plymouth
Diocese created 1850, covers Cornwall, Devon and Dorset
Named for the Virgin Mary and St Boniface, said to be born in Crediton
Hosts annual naval mass for HMNB Devonport personnel each July

w: This south-facing sweep of open ground sits above low limestone cliffs, commanding views across Plymouth Sound to Drake's Island and Mount Edgcumbe beyond. Its name comes from the Anglo-Saxon hoh, a heel-shaped sloping ridge - the same root behind the place name Sutton Hoo.
s: The clifftop green with views clear to Drake's Island
_facts: South-facing open public space above low limestone cliffs
Views of Plymouth Sound, Drake's Island and Mount Edgcumbe
Name from Anglo-Saxon hoh (sloping ridge), same root as Sutton Hoo

w: Seat of the Edgcumbe family since Tudor times, this stately home overlooking Plymouth Sound is Grade II listed while its gardens and parkland rank Grade I - a rare case of an estate's grounds outranking its house. Richard Edgcumbe was made Baron Edgcumbe in 1742, and his son George was advanced to Earl in 1789.
s: A house outranked by its own gardens
_facts: Principal seat of the Edgcumbe family since Tudor times
House Grade II listed; gardens and parkland Grade I
Richard Edgcumbe made Baron Edgcumbe in 1742
Son George advanced to Earl in 1789

w: Sir Bernard de Gomme built this citadel in the late 1660s on the site of an earlier fort raised in Sir Francis Drake's time, at the eastern end of Plymouth Hoe overlooking the Sound. It remains a Scheduled Monument with Grade II listed buildings inside, still an active military site rather than a museum piece.
s: A 1660s fortress built over Francis Drake's own fort
_facts: Built in the late 1660s, designed by Sir Bernard de Gomme
Replaced an earlier fort dating from Sir Francis Drake's time
At the eastern end of Plymouth Hoe, overlooking Plymouth Sound
Scheduled Monument; buildings within are Grade II listed

w: Opened in 1917 as a Royal Navy seaplane station on this peninsula in Plymouth Sound, it became RAF Cattewater the following year and was renamed in 1928 for Captain Batten, a Civil War commander who once defended the site. Little remains today beyond memorials, road names, the original slipway and two Grade II listed 1917 aeroplane hangars.
s: A seaplane base reduced to two 1917 hangars and a slipway
_facts: Opened 1917 as Royal Navy Air Service Station Cattewater
Became RAF Cattewater in 1918, renamed RAF Mount Batten in 1928
Named for Captain Batten, an English Civil War commander
Surviving remains: original slipway and two Grade II listed 1917 hangars

w: Opened in May 1998 near the Barbican and fish market, this is the largest aquarium in the UK, home to more than 5,000 animals. Run by the Ocean Conservation Trust, it doubles as an educational charity teaching visitors about the marine environment rather than a purely commercial attraction.
s: The UK's biggest aquarium, run by a conservation charity
_facts: Opened May 1998 near Sutton Harbour
Largest aquarium in the UK
Houses over 5,000 animals
Run by the Ocean Conservation Trust, a charity

w: One of Lord Palmerston's ring of forts built in the 1860s to defend Plymouth, Crownhill Fort has been restored by the Landmark Trust into small businesses, museums and a holiday apartment sleeping eight. It opens to the public on the last Friday of every month, plus tours for local schools and societies.
s: A Victorian fort turned museum, offices and holiday let
_facts: Palmerston fort built in the 1860s
Restored by the Landmark Trust
Houses businesses, museums, exhibitions and a holiday apartment sleeping eight
Open to the public on the last Friday of each month

w: Built after the 1859 Royal Commission on National Defence to guard Plymouth's north-east approaches, this Palmerston fort once carried fifteen guns and five mortars behind a barrack block for sixty men. Sold to the council in 1958 and Grade II listed in 2008, it now serves as a Thai Buddhist temple.
s: A Victorian gun fort reborn as a Buddhist temple
_facts: Built after the 1859 Royal Commission on National Defence
Armed with fifteen guns and five mortars
Sold to Plymouth City Council in 1958; Grade II listed in 2008
Now a Thai Buddhist temple

w: Opened in 1898 as a music hall, gutted by fire within three months, then rebuilt as a Flemish Renaissance variety theatre with an Art Nouveau, nautical-themed interior. It became a bingo hall in 1961, a theatre again, then a disco, and finally closed after a drugs raid - now a Grade II* listed building slowly decaying while its future is decided.
s: Music hall, bingo hall, disco, drug bust, now derelict
_facts: Opened 1898 as a music hall; damaged by fire within three months
Flemish Renaissance exterior, Art Nouveau nautical interior
Became a bingo hall in 1961, later a disco, then closed after a drugs raid
Grade II* listed, on the buildings-at-risk register
